practices: Look at the raw file (cat/type) before choosing read_csv arguments (p.168).
Use header=None with names=[...] when the file has no header row (p.169).
Use index_col with a list of names to build a hierarchical index (p.170).
Use sep='\s+' (a regex) for whitespace-separated files (p.171).
Use skiprows for comment or junk lines (p.171).
Use na_values, as a list or per-column dict, for custom missing-value sentinels (p.172).
Use nrows to sample a big file and chunksize to iterate through it, aggregating piece by piece (p.174).
Use to_csv with na_rep, index=False, header=False, columns= to control output (p.175-176).
Use the csv module with a Dialect or keyword args for malformed single-character-delimited files; fall back to str.split or re.split for multi-character delimiters (p.176-178).
Build DataFrames from lists of dicts parsed from JSON, selecting columns; use to_json(orient='records') for row-wise output (p.179-180).
Use read_html to extract <table> elements into a list of DataFrames; use lxml.objectify for general XML (p.180-183).
Use pickle only for short-term storage; consider HDF5 or Feather for larger or cross-language needs (p.184-185).
Use HDFStore format='table' when you need queries (slower than 'fixed'); avoid concurrent writers (p.185-186).
Use requests plus resp.json() for web APIs and pass the list of dicts to DataFrame (p.187).
Use read_sql with a SQLAlchemy engine instead of building DataFrames from fetchall and cursor.description (p.190).
